chastise

/chas-TYZE/ - rhymes with prize · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Chastise means to criticize or rebuke severely.

The league formally chastised the club for fielding an ineligible player, and the statement stayed pinned to its website all season.

Example

The dean summoned the fraternity's officers and chastised them for the damaged statue, reading the restoration bill aloud line by line.

Chastise is severe, deliberate rebuke — harsher than admonish, more controlled than berating's shouting, and often official. It tends to come from authority, land on the record, and leave a mark that outlasts the conversation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

castigate: To castigate is to reprimand severely, often before an audience — chastise's near-twin, and the two overlap heavily. The shade of difference: castigate leans toward the public lashing, delivered for onlookers, while chastise leans official — the severe rebuke from authority that lands on the record and stays there.

discipline: To discipline is to correct with penalties, and it can be entirely neutral and procedural — a matter of policy, with no anger in it. Chastise is the rebuke itself: severe words from authority, condemnation put on the record. You can be disciplined without a single harsh word; to chastise is to say the harsh words.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

laud: praise formally and warmly

excuse: let a fault pass without blame

Where it sits · how savagely the fault is called out — correct → chastise → excoriate

correct vs. chastise: To correct someone is neutral repair, far milder than chastise's severe rebuke.

excoriate vs. chastise: Excoriate goes further than chastise — criticism so savage it strips the skin off in public.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — chast

Root — chast: pure (Latin castus)

Suffix — -ise

Suffix — -ise: verb ending: to make

Put it together

Put it together: Chast (pure) + -ise (to make) = to make pure. Latin castigare was to correct someone into purity; chastise remembers that severe correction once claimed to be a cleansing — punishment sold as improvement.

Use the root in a new word: chasten

Use the root in a new word: chasten: The narrow loss chastened the champions, scrubbing the swagger out of them for the rest of the season.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal

Chastise suits severe, often official rebuke — boards, deans, tribunals. In this unit's scolding family, admonish corrects without condemnation and berate adds volume but less authority; chastise lands hardest on the record. Its formal cousin censure — a body's voted disapproval — appears in this unit's reference list.
